Learning Objectives
Learn the anatomic components of the elbow.
Understand how the bony and soft-tissue structures contribute to elbow stability.

Trochoginglymoid joint
Figure 1 Illustrations show the anatomy of the elbow and forearm. (Reproduced from Abboud JA:
Elbow and forearm, in Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 5.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, p 366.) View image full screen

Components
The elbow joint consists of the distal humerus, proximal ulna, and proximal radius. It is a
trochoginglymoid joint with three articulations: the ulnohumeral joint, radiohumeral
joint, and proximal radioulnar joint. The ulnohumeral joint is highly congruous and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Elbow Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000584
2/30

provides hinge motion (ginglymoid) with flexion-extension. The radiohumeral and
proximal radioulnar joints allow rotation (trochoid) with pronation-supination. The
articular surfaces are irregular in shape and provide inherent osseous stability because
of their anatomic congruency1 (Resource 3).
Distal Humerus
Trochlea and capitellum (Figure 2)
The articular surface has approximately 30° of anterior tilt, 3° to 5° of internal rotation, and 4°
to 8° of valgus.
Figure 2 Cadaver model dissection photographs of an elbow show distal humeral articular
angulation in anterior (A) and posterior (B) views in the coronal plane and sagittal plane (C).
(Reproduced from Morrey ME: Anatomy, biomechanics, physical examination, and imaging of the
elbow, in Parvizi J, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update, ed 13. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 321-340.)

Distal Humerus
The distal humerus articular surface consists of the trochlea and the capitellum. The
trochlea is an articular cylinder (spool) between the lateral and medial metaphyseal
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Elbow Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000584
3/30

flares (columns) of the distal humerus. It is centered in line with the long axis of the
humeral shaft. The articular surface has approximately 30° of anterior tilt, 3° to 5° of
internal rotation, and 4° to 8° of valgus. The capitellum is lateral to the trochlea and
articulates with the radial head. The trochlea has a high degree of articular congruency
with the greater sigmoid notch of the olecranon. The olecranon fossa receives the tip of
the olecranon during terminal extension, whereas the coronoid fossa receives the
coronoid tip in flexion, and the radial fossa receives the radial head in flexion. The lateral
condyle serves as the origin for the lateral collateral ligaments (LCLs). The medial
epicondyle serves as the origin for the medial collateral ligaments (MCLs).
Proximal Radius
The radial head is a secondary stabilizer to valgus stress (Figure 3).
Cartilage encircles approximately 280° of the radial head.
The lateral 80° is a safe zone for screw placement.
Figure 3 Cadaver model dissection photographs show the elbow joint articulation. A, Exposed
through the capsule with the relevant bony landmarks and ligamentous attachment sites
identified. B, The 15° of angular tilt from the long axis of the radius at the level of the radial
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Elbow Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000584
4/30

tuberosity through the radial head and neck. C, The ellipsoid radial head and annular ligament
articulating with the lesser sigmoid notch within the proximal radioulnar joint. The greater
sigmoid notch and the bare area also are identified in relationship to the olecranon tip and the
coronoid processes medial and lateral facets. LUCL = lateral ulnar collateral ligament, MUCL =
medial ulnar collateral ligament, RCL = radial collateral ligament. (Reproduced from Morrey ME:
Anatomy, biomechanics, physical examination, and imaging of the elbow, in Parvizi J, ed:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update, ed 13. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2021, pp 321-340.)

Proximal Radius
The radial head is an important secondary stabilizer to valgus stress, particularly in MCL-
deficient elbows. The radial head is elliptical and variably offset from the radial neck. The
concavity of the radial head articulates with the hemispheric capitellum. Cartilage
encircles approximately 280° of the radial head, with the lateral 80° (safe zone) devoid of
cartilage. This is an important consideration for the placement of internal fixation for
radial head and neck fractures. The radial neck is angled approximately 15° from the
long axis of the radial shaft. The proximal radial tuberosity provides the insertion site for
the distal biceps tendon.
Proximal Ulna
The sagittal ridge of the greater sigmoid notch articulates with the apex of the trochlea (Figure
4).
The crista supinatoris (supinator crest) provides insertion of the lateral ulnar collateral
ligament (UCL).
The sublime tubercle provides insertion for the anterior bundle of the MCL.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Elbow Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000584
5/30

Figure 4 Cadaver model dissection photograph of an elbow shows proximal ulnar articular
angulation in the sagittal plane. (Reproduced from Morrey ME: Anatomy, biomechanics, physical
examination, and imaging of the elbow, in Parvizi J, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update, ed 13.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 321-340.)

Proximal Ulna
The ulnohumeral joint is the major osseous stabilizer of the elbow joint. The sagittal
ridge of the greater sigmoid notch articulates with the apex of the trochlea. The coronoid
acts as an anterior buttress to posterior dislocation and provides increased stability with
the elbow in flexion. The transverse sulcus at the midportion of the articular surface of
the olecranon is normally devoid of cartilage. The crista supinatoris (supinator crest) on
the lateral side of the ulna serves as the insertion site for the lateral UCL and the origin
of the supinator muscle. The sublime tubercle on the medial side of the ulna is the
insertion site for the anterior bundle of the MCL. The lesser sigmoid notch articulates
with the rim of the radial head. The olecranon tip rotates into the olecranon fossa during
elbow extension. The angle created with a line from the coronoid tip through the
olecranon tip compared to the long axis of the ulna is approximately 30°. The slight
proximal ulna dorsal angulation must also be accounted for during reduction of
fractures or management of malunions.2

LCL Complex

Figure 6 Photograph of an elbow shows the lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL) complex. The
lines represent the approximate orientations of the radial collateral ligament (RCL) and LUCL on
the lateral side of the elbow. The yellow outline is the location of the annular ligament
attachment proximal and deep to the ligamentous complex but intimately associated with it. The
blue outline represents the ligamentous attachment site on the ulna of the LUCL proper.
(Reproduced from Morrey ME: Anatomy, biomechanics, physical examination, and imaging of the
elbow, in Parvizi J, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update, ed 13. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 321-340.)

LCL Complex
The LCL complex acts as a functional unit to provide posterolateral and varus stability to
the elbow. The lateral UCL acts as the primary stabilizer to posterolateral rotatory
instability. It originates along the lateral condyle and inserts onto the crista supinatoris
on the ulna. Relatively uniform tension is present in the ligament throughout the arc of
flexion-extension4 (Resource 5).
The annular ligament stabilizes the proximal radioulnar joint. It attaches to the anterior
and posterior margins of the lesser sigmoid notch. The radial collateral ligament
attaches to the anterior and posterior margins of the lesser sigmoid notch. The
accessory collateral ligament attaches to the annular ligament and the crista supinatoris.

MCL Complex 

MCL Complex
The MCL complex consists of the anterior and posterior bundles and the transverse
ligament (sometimes referred to as the oblique bundle)3,5(Figures 7 and 8; Resource 6).
Figure 7 Illustration of the medial aspect of the elbow shows the medial collateral
ligament complex. (Reproduced from Gramstad G: Anatomy of the shoulder, arm, and
elbow, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 715-726.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Elbow Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000584
9/30

Figure 8 Photograph of an elbow shows that the medial ulnar collateral ligaments are
areas of capsular thickening that provide stability to the medial side of the elbow joint.
The red dashed line is the anterior band of the anterior bundle, the dotted black line is
the posterior band of the anterior bundle, the blue dotted line is the posterior bundle,
and the yellow dotted line is the transverse bundle. (Reproduced from Morrey ME:
Anatomy, biomechanics, physical examination, and imaging of the elbow, in Parvizi J, ed:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update, ed 13. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2021, pp 321-340.)
The anterior bundle is the primary stabilizer to valgus stress and is the most distinct
structure of the MCL complex. The anterior bundle often referred is to as the medial UCL
or the UCL. The origin of the ligament is at the anteroinferior surface of the medial
epicondyle. It inserts onto the sublime tubercle at the anteromedial coronoid process.
The anterior bundle can be divided into three bands: anterior, central, and posterior. The
anterior band is more vulnerable to valgus stress in extension, whereas the posterior
band is more vulnerable to valgus stress in flexion. The central band is the most
isometric throughout the arc of flexion-extension6,7 (Figure 9; Resource 7).

Figure 9 Cadaver model specimen of a left elbow (medial view) shows the transverse
bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament.1, Transverse bundle of the ulnar collateral
ligament. 2, Anterior bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament. 3, Anterior common tendon.
4, Medial epicondyle of the humerus. 5, Sublime tubercle of the ulna. D = distal, P =
proximal. (Reproduced with permission from Edama M, Matsuzawa K, Yokota H, et al:
Elbow valgus stability of the transverse bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament. BMC
Musculoskelet Disord 202112;22[1]:873.)
The posterior bundle is primarily a capsular thickening that also forms the floor of the
cubital tunnel. The posterior bundle limits elbow flexion if contracted and may be
divided during contracture release.
The transverse ligament extends from the top of the olecranon to the coronoid. It also
has been described as a capsular thickening that is thought to provide minimal stability
to the elbow joint.

Capsule
The anterior capsule is taut in extension, and the posterior capsule is taut in flexion.

Capsule
The capsule of the elbow joint attaches along the articular margin. The anterior capsule
extends proximal to the coronoid and the radial fossae, distal to the coronoid process,
and lateral to the annular ligament. The posterior capsule extends proximal to the
olecranon fossa, medial and lateral along the articular margins of the greater sigmoid
notch, and lateral to the annular ligament. The anterior capsule is taut in extension, and
the posterior capsule is taut in flexion. This is important to understand for restoration of
elbow motion in patients undergoing capsular release.
Intracapsular pressure is lowest at 70° to 80° of elbow flexion. Capsular volume is 25 to
30 mL if fully distended.
Muscles and Tendons
Musculature
Four primary groups1
Elbow flexors
Biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis
Biceps also is primary forearm supinator
Elbow extensors
Triceps
Forearm flexor-pronators
Forearm extensors
Anconeus
Dynamic constraint to varus and posterolateral rotatory instability
The origin, insertion, innervation, and action of the muscles of the elbow are shown in the


Musculature
Muscles that cross the elbow joint provide dynamic stability to the joint. By compression
of the joint, these muscles can help protect the soft-tissue constraints. The muscles that
originate near the elbow joint provide primarily forearm, wrist, and hand function, and
have a lesser effect on elbow flexion and extension. Although the muscles originating
near the joint may also contribute as dynamic stabilizers, their tendinous origins more
importantly contribute as secondary static stabilizers.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Elbow Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000584
13/30

The common flexor origin, including the origin of the pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis,
palmaris longus, flexor carpi ulnaris, and flexor digitorum superficialis, provide valgus
restraint. The common extensor origin, including the origin of the extensor carpi radialis
longus, extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor digitorum communis, extensor digiti
minimi, and extensor carpi ulnaris, provide varus restraint. The anconeus is unique in
that its primary function is dynamic stability rather than skeletal motion.
Nerves
Lateral Antebrachial Cutaneous Nerve
Terminal branch of the musculocutaneous nerve

Lateral Antebrachial Cutaneous Nerve
The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve is the terminal branch of the
musculocutaneous nerve from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus. The
musculocutaneous nerve runs between the biceps and the brachialis and provides
innervation to these muscles. It then emerges lateral to the distal biceps tendon and
continues as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. It is sometime referred to as the
lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. This nerve is at risk during anterior surgical
exposure for distal biceps tendon repair.
Radial Nerve
Travels with the profunda brachii artery in the spiral groove on the posterior humerus
Pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to enter the anterior compartment of the arm
Terminates into superficial and deep branches
The deep branch is known as the posterior interosseous nerve.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Elbow Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000584
14/30


Radial Nerve
The radial nerve is the termination of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus along with
the axillary nerve. The radial nerve passes through the triangular interval posterior to
the shoulder. This anatomic landmark is bordered by the humeral shaft laterally, the
long head of the triceps medially, and the teres major proximally. It travels between the
lateral and medial heads of the triceps in the spiral groove on the posterior humerus,
the location at which it is at risk of injury from humeral shaft fractures. For much of its
course through the posterior arm, the nerve travels with the profunda brachii artery. At
the level of the deltoid insertion, the nerve is directly posterior in the arm. As the nerve
continues laterally, distal to the deltoid insertion, it pierces the lateral intermuscular
septum to enter the anterior compartment of the arm, approximately at the junction of
the middle and distal third of the humerus. It passes superficial to the elbow joint
capsule near the radiocapitellar joint, the location at which it is at risk during
arthroscopic procedures. The radial nerve then divides and terminates into a superficial
and a deep branch. The superficial branch is sensory and provides cutaneous
innervation to the dorsum of the hand. The deep branch often is referred to as the
posterior interosseous nerve and provides motor innervation to the muscles in the
posterior forearm. It crosses the proximal radial shaft as it pierces through the supinator
and is at risk during exposure and retraction around the proximal radius.
Ulnar Nerve
Enters the posterior compartment of the brachium through the medial intermuscular septum
at the arcade of Struthers8 (Resource 8)
Passes through the cubital tunnel posterior to the medial epicondyle

Ulnar Nerve
The ulnar nerve is a continuation of the medial cord of the brachial plexus. It travels in
the posteromedial arm and pierces through the medial intermuscular septum at the
arcade of Struthers. It courses posterior to the medial epicondyle through the cubital
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Elbow Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000584
15/30

tunnel, giving off an articular branch that aids in proprioception. The floor of the cubital
tunnel is formed by the posterior bundle of the MCL, whereas the fascia of the flexor
carpi ulnaris forms the roof of the tunnel. Elbow flexion has been shown to decrease the
volume of the cubital tunnel and elongate the nerve, leading to ulnar neuropathy from
nerve compression and tension.8 The first motor branch of the ulnar nerve branches
distal to the cubital tunnel, innervating the flexor carpi ulnaris.
Median Nerve (Lateral and Medial Cords)
Located medial to the brachial artery in the cubital fossa

Median Nerve (Lateral and Medial Cords)
The median nerve emerges from the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus. It is
located lateral to the brachial artery in the proximal arm, then crosses over about
halfway down to continue medial to the artery. It continues through the anterior elbow
medial to the brachial artery in the cubital fossa. It proceeds to the forearm under the
bicipital aponeurosis and between the two heads of the pronator teres. It travels distally
to innervate the muscles of the volar forearm and hand as the anterior interosseous
nerve and the palmar cutaneous nerve.
Ligament of Struthers and Arcade of Struthers
Ligament of Struthers can compress the medial nerve and brachial artery
Arcade of Struthers can compress the ulnar nerve

Ligament of Struthers and Arcade of Struthers
The arcade of Struthers often is confused with the ligament of Struthers. Although both
eponyms are attributed to the distinguished Scottish anatomist and surgeon, Sir John
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Elbow Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000584
16/30

Struthers (1823-1899), they are two distinct anatomic structures related to different
nerves.9
The perhaps more well-known ligament of Struthers was first coined by Sir John
Struthers in 1854, referring to a ligamentous or muscular structure (often an extension
of the humeral head of the pronator teres muscle) passing between the medial
epicondyle and supracondylar process of the humerus. It is found in approximately 1%
of individuals and may result in median nerve and/or brachial artery entrapment.
The arcade of Struthers was not described until 1973; although attributed to Sir John
Struthers, it was never found to be mentioned in his writings. The term is used to
describe a thickening of the anteromedial aspect of the medial intermuscular septum,
which forms a myofibrous sheath around the ulnar nerve as it passes from the anterior
to the posterior compartment of the arm through the septum. It sometimes is defined as
a canal on the medial aspect of the middle and lower third of the arm, consisting of the
medial head of the triceps brachii muscle and its aponeurotic expansion, which extends
into the intermuscular septum and the internal brachial ligament and covers part of the
ulnar nerve. Although some dispute its presence as a distinct structure, it has been
reported in 50% to 100% of specimens. Some surgeons consider it to be a site of ulnar
nerve entrapment, while others consider it to be more of a secondary site of nerve
entrapment after ulnar nerve transposition.10,11
Vascular Anatomy
Brachial Artery
Descends in the anterior compartment of the arm with the median nerve
At the level of the elbow joint, the brachial artery branches into the radial and ulnar arteries.

Brachial Artery
The brachial artery is a continuation of the axillary artery that descends in the anterior
arm with the medial nerve. Proximally, the brachial artery is medial to the medial nerve.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Elbow Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000584
17/30

The nerve crosses to become medial to the artery halfway down the arm. Immediately
distal to the teres major, the brachial artery gives off a deep branch, the profunda
brachial artery, which travels in the posterior arm with the radial nerve. The brachial
artery enters the cubital fossa under the bicipital aponeurosis and bifurcates into the
radial and ulnar arteries.
Arthroscopic Anatomy of the Elbow
The close proximity of neurovascular structures places them at risk of injury during
arthroscopy4,12 (Figures 10, 11, and 12; Video 1; Resource 9).
The radial nerve is at risk from the proximal anterolateral portal.
The ulnar nerve is at risk from the proximal anteromedial portal.
The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve is at risk from the anteromedial portal.
The average distance between the medial portal and the median nerve is greater than the
distance between the lateral portal and the radial nerve or posterior interosseous nerve.13
The radial nerve lies close to the anterior capsule at the mid-aspect of the radiocapitellar joint.

Arthroscopic Anatomy of the Elbow
Safe and effective elbow arthroscopy requires a thorough understanding of the adjacent
neurovascular structures and careful portal placement. Surface landmarks to be
identified include the olecranon, medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, medial
intramuscular septum, lateral supracondylar ridge, and radial head and its articulation
with the capitellum.
Distension of the joint prior to portal placement is a crucial step because it increases the
distance of the neurovascular structures from the articular surface to decrease the risk
of iatrogenic injury. A transient ulnar nerve palsy is the most common neurologic
complication after elbow arthroscopy. The ulnar nerve is located directly superficial to
the joint capsule in the posterior medial gutter.14
The ulnar nerve is located approximately 3 to 4 mm from the proximal anteromedial
portal. The nerve is located posterior to the intermuscular septum; therefore, care must
be taken to ensure the portal remains anterior to the intermuscular septum. The
surgeon also should carefully examine whether the ulnar nerve subluxates with flexion
and extension. The nerve is at risk if it subluxates anteriorly with elbow flexion because it
is no longer protected by the medial intermuscular septum. The medial antebrachial
cutaneous nerve is most at risk from the anteromedial portal, and portal incisions
should be just through the dermis and not deep into the subcutaneous tissue to prevent
injury to the nerve. The anterolateral portal places the radial nerve at substantial risk of
iatrogenic injury. A proximal anterolateral portal often is used in favor of the direct
lateral portal because the risk of neurovascular injury decreases as the portal is moved
more proximally13 (Resource 10).
The intra-articular anatomy of the elbow can be divided into three distinct
compartments. The anterior compartment contains the coronoid process, anterior
trochlea, radial head, anterior capitellum, coronoid and radial fossa, and medial and
lateral condyles. The posterior compartment contains the olecranon tip, olecranon fossa,

posterior trochlea, and medial and lateral gutters. The posterior lateral compartment
contains the radial head, olecranon, lateral gutter, and posterior capitellum15 (Resource
11).
The origin of the extensor carpi radialis brevis can be accessed intra-articularly and
released arthroscopically. The footprint is diamond-shaped, measuring 13 mm × 7 mm,
and is located just beneath the distalmost tip of the lateral supracondylar ridge. It is
tendinous in this area, whereas the extensor carpi radialis longus is muscular along the
lateral supracondylar ridge.12 The lateral UCL, located deep to the extensor carpi radialis
brevis, is at risk for iatrogenic injury during arthroscopic débridement for lateral
epicondylitis.
Contributions to Elbow Stability
Dynamic and Static Constraints
Static stabilizers include inherent bony stability, capsule, and ligaments (Figure 13).
Primary static constraints: ulnohumeral articulation, LCL complex, anterior bundle of the
MCL
Secondary static constraints: radiocapitellar articulation, common flexor origin, common
extensor origin, capsule
Dynamic stabilizers include muscles that across the elbow joint.

Figure 13 Schematic shows how the static constraints in the elbow are analogous to the defenses
of a fortress. The primary static constraints to elbow instability are the ulnohumeral articulation,

the capsule, the radiocapitellar articulation, and the common flexor and extensor tendon origins.


Dynamic and Static Constraints
Stability of the elbow is provided by static and dynamic constraints. The static
constraints have been described as analogous to a fortress. The primary static
constraints are the congruent bony anatomy of the ulnohumeral articulation, LCL
complex, and anterior bundle of the MCL. Secondary static constraints include the
radiocapitellar articulation, common flexor origin, common extensor origin, and capsule.

The capsule has been shown to provide the most stabilizing effect with the elbow in
extension16 (Resource 12).
Dynamic constraints include muscles that cross the elbow joint, such as the anconeus,
triceps, biceps, and brachialis. These stabilizers provide a variable degree of compressive
forces with a net posterior vector.
Forearm Rotation
The LCL-deficient elbow is more stable in pronation.1
The MCL-deficient elbow is more stable in supination.

Forearm Rotation
The exact mechanism of forearm rotation as it relates to elbow stability is unclear.
Forearm pronation has been hypothesized to rotate the radial head more proximally,
increasing the contact at the radiocapitellar joint and providing increased posterolateral
stability. Forearm supination may lead to increased tension in the flexor pronator mass,
providing additional valgus stability.
Osseous Congruency

Osseous Congruency
Coronoid fractures that are greater than 50% increase varus-valgus laxity and may lead
to posterolateral rotatory instability. The radial head contributes as much as 30% to the
valgus stability of the elbow. This is most important in MCL-deficient elbows. If the radial
head is resected, the MCL becomes the primary constraint to valgus instability.1,16

Biomechanical Features of the Elbow
Flexion-Extension
Axis is from the anteroinferior medial epicondyle through the center of the trochlea, and the
center of the capitellum
Requirements for activities of daily living 30° to 130°

Flexion-Extension
Motion from the elbow joint is relatively constrained. It consists of flexion-extension and
pronation-supination to position the forearm and hand. The axis of rotation is from the
anteroinferior medial epicondyle passing through the center of the trochlea to the
center of the capitellum. The axis of flexion-extension is 4° to 8° of valgus relative to the
long axis of the humerus and 3° to 5° of internal rotation relative to the medial and
lateral epicondylar access. The normal arc of motion is approximately 0° to 140°.
Activities of daily living require 30° to 130° of flexion-extension.
Pronation-Supination
Axis is from the center of radial head through center of the distal ulna
Activities of daily living require 100° of forearm rotation, with 50° of pronation to 50° of
supination.

Pronation-Supination
The axis of pronation-supination of the forearm extends from the center of the radial
head through the center of the distal ulna. The normal arc of motion is 180°, with 90° of
pronation to 90° of supination. The requirement for activities of daily living is 100°, with
50° of pronation to 50° of supination. Loss of pronation can be compensated by
shoulder abduction. There is no compensation for loss of supination.
